How cannabis legalization has impacted crime rates

Explore how cannabis legalization has impacted crime rates across the United States. Review the data on arrests, violent crime, and the broader effects on criminal justice.

By HowToEdibles Editorial TeamMarch 5, 2026Updated November 8, 20268 min read

Short answer

Most peer-reviewed studies find that legalizing cannabis has not increased violent or property crime overall. A time-series study of Colorado and Washington found "minimal to no effect on major crimes", and a Washington–Oregon border study found drops in rapes and property crimes. The clearest effect is far fewer cannabis arrests. Findings on crime near dispensaries are mixed.

Study Setting Main finding
Lu et al., Justice Quarterly (2019/2021) Colorado and Washington, recreational legalization and retail sales No statistically significant long-term effect on violent or property crime
Dragone et al., J. Economic Behavior & Organization (2019) Washington vs. Oregon border counties, 2010–2014 Significant drop in rapes and property crimes on the Washington side
Morris et al., PLOS ONE (2014) US states with medical marijuana laws, 1990–2006 No increase in any major (Part I) crime; possible drop in homicide and assault
Brinkman & Mok-Lamme, Regional Science and Urban Economics (2019) Denver neighborhoods Dispensaries linked to less crime in their immediate neighborhood
Hughes et al., Justice Quarterly (2019) Denver, 2012–2015 Dispensaries linked to more neighborhood crime and disorder (except murder and auto theft)

Few arguments in the cannabis legalization debate have been as contentious as the relationship between legal marijuana and crime. Opponents long warned that loosening cannabis laws would lead to spikes in violent crime, property theft, and public safety hazards. Proponents countered that legalization would reduce the burden on criminal justice systems and redirect law enforcement resources toward more serious offenses. Now, with more than a decade of data from states like Colorado and Washington — and a growing number of states following suit — researchers have a much clearer picture of what actually happened.

The pre-legalization landscape

To understand the impact of legalization on crime, it helps to understand what came before it. For decades, cannabis prohibition was one of the primary drivers of drug arrests in the United States. In 2010, according to an ACLU analysis of FBI data, there were 889,133 marijuana arrests nationwide, about 300,000 more than arrests for all violent crimes. The vast majority of these arrests, roughly 88%, were for simple possession rather than distribution or manufacturing.

The enforcement of cannabis laws was also deeply unequal. A landmark 2013 report by the American Civil Liberties Union found that Black Americans were 3.73 times more likely to be arrested for marijuana possession than white Americans, despite roughly equal rates of use across racial groups. In some counties, Black residents were more than 10, 15, or even 30 times more likely to be arrested. These arrests carried lasting consequences — criminal records that could block access to housing, employment, education, and public benefits for years or even decades after the fact.

The financial cost was staggering as well. The ACLU estimated that states collectively spent over $3.6 billion in 2010 enforcing marijuana possession laws. Critics argued that these resources would be far better spent addressing violent crime, property crime, and other threats to public safety.

Crime rates after legalization

When Colorado and Washington became the first states to legalize recreational cannabis in 2012, opponents predicted a wave of crime. More than a decade later, the data tells a different story. A study in the Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization compared border counties in Washington, which legalized at the end of 2012, with Oregon, which followed at the end of 2014. It found that legalization "caused a significant reduction in rapes and property crimes" on the Washington side in 2013–2014. Earlier, a 2014 PLOS ONE study of state data from 1990 to 2006 found that medical marijuana laws did not increase any major category of crime and may have been associated with lower homicide and assault rates.

Research led by Washington State University scholars, published in Justice Quarterly, used interrupted time-series analysis of crime in Colorado and Washington. It concluded that legalization and retail sales had "minimal to no effect on major crimes", with no statistically significant long-term effects on violent or property crime. A separate analysis by the Cato Institute reached similar conclusions, noting that dire predictions about legalization leading to crime waves had simply not materialized.

It is worth noting that crime trends are influenced by many factors — economic conditions, policing strategies, demographic shifts, and more. Isolating the effect of any single policy change is inherently difficult. However, the consistent finding across multiple studies and multiple states is clear: legalization has not been the crime catalyst that critics feared.

Impact on cannabis-related arrests

The most immediate and dramatic impact of legalization has been on cannabis-related arrests themselves. Adult possession within legal limits is no longer an arrestable offense in legal states, so low-level possession cases in Colorado and Washington fell steeply after 2012. Similar patterns have played out in other states that have legalized.

Nationally, the shift has been significant. Marijuana arrests have fallen far below the 2010 level of nearly 890,000, a decline driven largely by states adopting legalization or decriminalization measures. This represents hundreds of thousands of people each year who are no longer funneled into the criminal justice system for possessing a substance that most Americans believe should be legal. Gallup measured a record 70% support for legalization in October 2023.

The reduction in arrests has also eased the burden on courts, jails, and public defenders. In many jurisdictions, cannabis cases once constituted a significant portion of the criminal docket. Removing these cases has allowed the justice system to focus its limited resources on more serious matters.

Violent crime and property crime

One of the most persistent concerns about legalization has been whether legal cannabis businesses would attract violent crime — robberies targeting cash-heavy dispensaries, for example, or turf wars over market share. While dispensary robberies have occurred in some areas, research suggests these incidents have not driven broader increases in violent crime.

The evidence on dispensaries specifically is mixed. A 2019 study of Denver in Regional Science and Urban Economics (Brinkman and Mok-Lamme) found that "retail dispensaries lead to reduced crime in the neighborhoods where they are located". The effect was highly localized, which fits a security or policing explanation and the disruption of illicit sellers. Another 2019 Denver study in Justice Quarterly (Hughes, Schaible and Jimmerson) used a different statistical model. It found that both medical and recreational dispensaries were associated with statistically significant increases in neighborhood crime and disorder, except for murder and auto theft. The safest reading is that any effect is local and depends on how dispensaries are policed and secured.

The relationship between legalization and the illicit market also matters. By creating a regulated alternative to the black market, legalization has reduced the demand for illicit cannabis — and with it, the violence and criminal activity associated with underground drug trade. While the illicit market has not disappeared entirely, particularly in states with high taxes or overly restrictive licensing, the legal market has captured a significant share of cannabis sales and diminished the power of illegal operations.

Law enforcement resource reallocation

Beyond the direct impact on crime statistics, legalization has allowed law enforcement agencies to redirect their attention and budgets. Police departments in legalized states have reported that officers who previously spent significant time on marijuana enforcement — conducting searches, making arrests, processing evidence, and testifying in court — are now able to focus on violent crime, property crime, and community policing.

The fiscal benefits extend to the broader criminal justice system. States have saved millions of dollars in prosecution costs, incarceration expenses, and probation supervision by removing cannabis offenses from the criminal code. Meanwhile, cannabis tax revenue has generated billions of dollars that states have invested in education, public health, infrastructure, and — in some cases — programs specifically designed to repair the harms of the war on drugs.

Colorado, for instance, reports more than $3.2 billion in marijuana taxes and fees collected from February 2014 through August 2026, with portions allocated to school construction, substance abuse treatment, and youth prevention programs. Illinois directs a share of its cannabis tax revenue to a fund specifically designed to support communities most harmed by decades of disproportionate enforcement.

Social equity and expungement

Perhaps the most significant criminal justice impact of legalization has been the movement toward expunging past cannabis convictions. Recognizing that it would be unjust to allow some people to profit from legal cannabis while others remained burdened by criminal records for the same activity, many states have passed laws to clear past marijuana convictions.

Illinois became a national model when it passed the Cannabis Regulation and Tax Act in 2019, which included automatic expungement provisions for low-level cannabis offenses. California has dismissed or reduced more than 100,000 cannabis convictions under Proposition 64. New York's legalization law included provisions to automatically expunge records for offenses that are no longer crimes under the new law.

These expungement efforts have been life-changing for hundreds of thousands of individuals. A cannabis conviction can follow a person for life, affecting their ability to get a job, rent an apartment, access student loans, or even volunteer at their child's school. By clearing these records, states are acknowledging that the war on drugs imposed lasting harm on communities — particularly Black and Latino communities — and taking concrete steps to address that legacy.

Social equity programs in the cannabis industry itself are also part of this effort. States like Illinois, New York, and New Jersey have created licensing programs that prioritize applicants from communities disproportionately impacted by cannabis enforcement, offering reduced fees, technical assistance, and access to capital. While these programs have faced criticism for slow implementation, they represent an important recognition that legalization must address past harms, not just create new business opportunities.
